title: Using a dictionary
subtitle: look up, definition, part of speech
summary: Learn what a dictionary tells you about a word - spelling, pronunciation, part of speech, definition and examples - and how to look words up well.

lesson.heading: Which dictionary do I need?

left.label: A bilingual dictionary
left.text: **Bilingual** means it uses two languages. It is easy to understand, and quick and easy to use.
examples: A **bilingual** dictionary gives you the word in your own language.
It is quick when you just need the meaning.

right.label: A dictionary in English
right.text: It gives you reading practice in English and many more examples of how a word is used.
examples: An English dictionary gives you a **definition** and several examples.
It shows you the word partners that go with the word.

lesson.note: If possible, use both. Most good learner's dictionaries are also available online.

lesson.heading: Looking up a word
lesson.text: To **look up** a word means to find it in a dictionary. A **definition** explains the meaning of the word. The dictionary also tells you the **part of speech** - noun, verb, adjective, and so on.

examples.text: I'll **look up** the word in my dictionary.
*fun* (noun): enjoyment or pleasure, or something that gives you enjoyment.
She's great fun to be with. / Have fun!

lesson.heading: What the dictionary tells you about a word
rows: pronunciation
how you say the word, written in phonemic symbols
part of speech
noun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition ...
the noun is uncountable, e.g. fun
a definition
a short explanation of the meaning
examples in italics
real sentences that show how the word is used
bold italics
common word partners that go with the word
fixed phrases in bold
e.g. for fun, make fun of somebody

lesson.heading: Spelling and silent letters
lesson.text: A dictionary is the fastest way to check a spelling. It also shows you **silent letters** - letters you write but do not say. In the word *island* the letter 's' is silent.

examples.note: Three spellings that learners often get wrong.

examples.text: In **knee** you do not say the 'k'; in **comb** you do not say the 'b'.
Both **organise** and **organize** are possible in British English.
examples.note: The 'z' spelling is usual in American English.

lesson.heading: Defining words
lesson.text: **Defining words** are the words a dictionary uses to explain other words. Some of them are very common, so it helps to learn them first.

examples.text: My teacher has always **emphasised** the importance of a notebook.
examples.note: emphasise = give something more attention and importance
relating to = having a relationship with something

examples.text: Five million pounds is a large **amount** of money.
examples.note: amount = how much there is of something
official = done by the government or someone in authority

examples.text: People can **behave** strangely when they're nervous.
examples.note: behave = do or say things in a particular way

lesson.heading: How to use a dictionary well
lesson.text: Put a tick next to a word when you check it. Each time you come back to that page, **see** if you still remember it. When you meet a new word in a text, first try to **guess** the meaning, then use the dictionary to see if your guess was correct.

examples.text: Don't just read the definition - the examples show you how the word is used.
If a bilingual dictionary gives you two or three translations, check them in an English dictionary.

lesson.note: Many words have more than one meaning. The first meaning in the dictionary is not always the one you want.

lesson.heading: One word, four meanings: post
rows: the system for sending letters
Did you send the cheque by post?
letters and parcels you send or receive
We haven't had any post yet.
a job (formal)
He's applied for a post overseas.
a long piece of wood or metal in the ground
I tied the flag to a post.

lesson.text: Read all the meanings before you choose one. The meaning you want is often the second or third in the list.

exercises.prompt: I didn't know the word, so I had to ___ it up in my dictionary.
exercises.explanation: To look up a word is to find it in a dictionary.

options: a dictionary that uses two languages
a dictionary that is only online

exercises.prompt: Is the spelling right or wrong?
Which letter is silent in each word?
A sum is an ___ of money.
exercises.hint: (= how much there is of something)
exercises.explanation: Amount tells you how much there is of something.

exercises.prompt: To pretend is to ___ as if something is true when it is not.
exercises.hint: (= do or say things in a particular way)
exercises.explanation: Behave means do or say things in a particular way.

exercises.prompt: A certificate is an ___ document that shows something is true.
exercises.hint: (= done by the government or someone in authority)
exercises.explanation: Official = done by the government or someone in authority, like a passport.

exercises.prompt: In the dictionary, *not at all* is 'used instead of no or not to ___ what you are saying', as in *I'm not at all happy about it*.
exercises.explanation: Emphasise means give something more attention and importance.

exercises.prompt: Advice is an ___ noun, so we never say 'advices'.
exercises.explanation: [U] in a dictionary means the noun is uncountable.

exercises.prompt: We were at school together, so she's an ___ friend.
exercises.explanation: An old friend is one you have known for a long time. Other word partners: my best friend, a close friend.

exercises.prompt: The word *post* has four meanings. Match each sentence with the right one.

pairs.left: He's applied for a post overseas.
Did you send the cheque by post?
I tied the flag to a post.
pairs.right: a long piece of wood or metal

pairs.left: We haven't had any post yet.

exercises.prompt: What should you do before you open your dictionary?
exercises.answer: First try to guess the meaning of the new word.
exercises.explanation: Guess first, then check with the dictionary to see if your guess was correct.

exercises.statement: A puppy is a very young dog.
exercises.explanation: Correct. This is the definition you find in a dictionary.
